Bulk capacitor lead cutting & forming · for THT through-hole assembly

Bulk capacitors in.
PCB-ready leads out.

S-EPCOS is a non-standard bulk capacitor lead cutting and forming machine built on an eight-station indexer. Loose capacitors ride a vibratory rail into lead cutting, an X-direction 90° form, a Y-direction 90° form, K-leg forming and a secondary reshaping pass — and leave on a conveyor at about 1,000 pieces an hour. The die set is cut to your capacitor drawing, so part ten matches part one thousand.

01 — Why it matters

Hand-formed leads are a tolerance you cannot audit

A lever and a hand jig take the operator out of the design of the part and put them back in the middle of it. Cut length drifts, the X and Y bends open or close with the wrist, and the K-leg changes shape between shifts. This machine exists to move that tolerance out of the operator’s hands and into a die cut to your drawing.

1

Cut length drifts on a hand jig

A lever jig cuts to a stop, not to a dimension. The stop wears, the lead springs, and the length that leaves the bench is a distribution rather than a number. You only see it at the insertion machine.

2

Two operators produce two populations

The same jig in two pairs of hands gives two interleaved distributions of parts. Averages pass incoming inspection while the insertion machine rejects parts from both, and the operator gets blamed for a fixture fault.

3

Bulk parts have no orientation to start with

Loose capacitors arrive randomly oriented, and a person has to pick and orient each one before it can be formed. That pick-and-orient step is the part of manual forming that scales worst, because it cannot be improved by practice.

02 — The process

Eight stations, one pass, no re-handling

The machine uses an indexer rotary-disc architecture assembled from four parts: the main machine, the vibratory feed rail, the cabinet and the control system. The working sequence below is quoted from the technical agreement, step for step.

Documented working sequence

#Step
1Bulk capacitors loaded into the rail
2Travel along the vibratory rail
3Stopper pre-locates the part
4Manipulator picks the part
5Part located
6Lead cutting
7X-direction 90° forming
8Y-direction 90° forming
9K-leg forming
10Secondary reshaping
11Discharge to conveyor
1

Loading structure

Manual feeding with vibratory alignment and discharge. A material sensor confirms the part has reached position and releases the next machine action.

2

Cutting station

Upper and lower cutting dies with a scrap chute under the tooling. The lead is cut as a discrete step, so the forming stations only have to hold form rather than length.

3

Forming station

Front and rear bending, a dedicated K-leg station and a reshaping station. Splitting the bends across stations is what keeps each dimension independent of the others.

4

Collection station

A feed conveyor carries finished parts to a collection tray, so the operator who keeps the bowl supplied is not also the operator who sorts the output.

03 — The machine

Four parts, one integrated cabinet

The agreement describes the machine as a rotary-disc indexer assembled from the main machine, the vibratory feed rail, the cabinet and the control system. Everything that touches the capacitor is either a die or a bowl, and both are made for your part.

1

Main machine

Indexer rotary-disc body carrying the eight stations, the cutting dies and the forming tooling. Tooling is cut to the capacitor drawing supplied with the enquiry.

2

Vibratory feed rail

Bowl and linear rail that take randomly oriented bulk capacitors and present them one at a time, in a known orientation, to the manipulator. Speed is set from a separate controller.

3

Cabinet

Integrated frame that carries the machine, the tooling and the scrap chute as one unit. The machine ships as a single item rather than as an assembly of stands.

4

Control system

Main control panel that sequences the indexer, the material sensor and the stations, and stops the machine when the material position is not confirmed.

11 — Insights

Eight reads on forming parts that have to fit

Written the way we explain it on the phone: the thing you notice first, the problem underneath it, a method you can reuse, the tool that carries the method, the reason to check again, and the one thing to do next. Articles are in English; headlines and standfirsts follow your language.

ARTICLE 01Cut length drift is a tooling problem, not a skill problem

Hand-forming loose capacitors looks like a training issue. It is not. The part moves because the fixture moves, and the fix is a die, not a lecture.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine figures quoted inside them come from the S-EPCOS technical agreement; part dimensions come from the customer’s capacitor drawing.

Watch the bench for ten minutes. The operator picks a capacitor out of the bag, drops it into the hand jig, pulls the lever, drops the finished part into a bin, and picks up the next one. Nothing in that motion is wrong. The operator is not the variable. The tenth part and the thousandth part come off the same lever, and they do not come off the same size.

That is the real cost of hand forming. Cut length wanders by a few tenths, the X and Y ninety-degree bends open or close depending on how hard the lever was pulled, and the K-leg shape changes with the operator's wrist. You find out at the insertion machine, where the leads no longer line up with the holes, and the parts get rejected one at a time. The rejection rate is not a mystery. It is a tolerance that was never held, measured on a jig that was never designed to hold it.

Here is the method that fixes it, and it costs nothing to try. Take ten formed parts at random from a shift. Measure three things on each: cut length, bend-to-bend distance, and the leg angle. Write the numbers on a board. If the spread on any one of them is wider than the tolerance on your drawing, the process is not capable, no matter how good the operator is. Do it again after lunch and compare. Two boards, ten parts each, and you have an argument that survives the meeting.

The tool that carries this method is a die set cut to your capacitor drawing. On the S-EPCOS project machine, bulk capacitors arrive on a vibratory rail, an eight-station indexer carries them through lead cutting, an X-direction ninety-degree form, a Y-direction ninety-degree form, K-leg forming and a secondary reshaping pass, and the finished parts leave on a conveyor at about one thousand pieces an hour. The die is the part that holds the tolerance. The machine is just what moves the part past the die, eight times a second, without getting tired.

The reason to come back is that the check keeps paying. Run the ten-part measurement quarterly and it becomes an early-warning system rather than an audit: a new capacitor supplier, a resharpened die, a batch with slightly different lead plating all show up as a widening spread before they show up as rejected parts. Factories that re-measure catch drift while it is still a trend line.

If you want the measurement done for you, send a photograph of your forming drawing and twenty formed parts to info@smthelp.com. We will measure the spread, tell you which dimension is the one that will fail, and quote a die only if a die is actually the answer.

ARTICLE 02The four numbers on the drawing that decide every part

Most forming drawings carry four figures that do all the work. Read them in the right order and you know whether your process can hold the part before you cut any metal.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine figures quoted inside them come from the S-EPCOS technical agreement; part dimensions come from the customer’s capacitor drawing.

Pull out the drawing and find the four figures that matter. On the S-EPCOS customer drawing they are printed next to circled callouts: a bend radius of 1.3 millimetres on each of two bends, an outer radius no larger than 0.5 millimetres, a leg angle of ten degrees with half a degree of tolerance, and a maximum body envelope of 18.5 millimetres. Everything else on the sheet is context. These four decide whether the part goes into the board or into the reject bin.

The pain is that these numbers do not fail independently, they fail together. Cut the lead a little short and the leg angle has to open to reach the pad. Open the angle and the bend radius changes, because the material is being pulled rather than bent. Get the K-leg slightly wrong and the part sits proud of the board, and the wave solder bridges it. By the time a part is rejected you cannot tell which of the four moved first, and the argument on the floor is about who formed it rather than which dimension drifted.

The reusable method is to measure them in a fixed order, because the order tells you the cause. Body envelope first, because it is the only one you do not control. Then bend radius, because it sets the material condition for everything downstream. Then leg angle. Then cut length last, because a cut length that is wrong while the other three are right almost always means the lead was cut before it was formed. Four measurements, one sequence, and the fault localises itself.

A machine that forms on an indexer can hold all four at once because the sequence is mechanical rather than manual. The die is cut to the drawing, the cut happens at a dedicated station, and the X and Y bends and the K-leg are formed in separate stations so that each one only has to hold its own dimension. A secondary reshaping pass then takes the spring-back out. On the S-EPCOS machine that chain runs at roughly one thousand parts an hour, and every part sees the same four stations in the same order.

Come back to the drawing when the part changes, not when the parts start failing. The four numbers move whenever the PCB designer moves a pad, whenever the capacitor series changes, and whenever the board thickness changes. Keep a copy of the measured spread next to the drawing revision, and the next change takes an afternoon instead of a month.

Send the drawing and a photograph of the pad on the board to info@smthelp.com. We will mark the four dimensions we would hold, tell you which one we expect to be tight on your part, and show you where the die would need a change.

ARTICLE 03Two operators, two different K-legs

Put two people on the same jig for one shift and you get two populations of parts. Not because one is careless, but because a hand jig has no reference surface.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine figures quoted inside them come from the S-EPCOS technical agreement; part dimensions come from the customer’s capacitor drawing.

Give two operators the same hand jig, the same capacitor batch and the same shift, and then measure their output separately. The distributions do not overlap cleanly. One sits slightly long, one slightly short, and both are inside the drawing on average. The averages agree. The parts do not.

This is the failure mode that costs the most and shows up the least. Averages pass every incoming check, so the process looks fine on paper. What actually reaches the insertion machine is two interleaved populations, and the operator on the odd shift gets blamed for a problem that was built into the fixture. On a K-leg form the effect is worse than on a straight bend, because the K shape has three reference points and a hand jig typically constrains only one of them.

The method that settles it is a capability split. Take twenty parts from each operator, measure the same dimension on all forty, and plot them as two groups rather than one. If the groups are separated, the fixture is the cause. If the groups overlap but the combined spread is too wide, the fixture is still the cause, but the fix is a better reference rather than a different person. Either way the conversation moves off the operator and onto the tool, which is where it belongs.

The tool that ends the argument is a die with a hard reference. When the part is located against a die surface and the bend is produced by the die's own geometry, there is no wrist in the loop. The S-EPCOS machine carries each capacitor on an eight-station indexer, forms the X and Y ninety-degree bends and the K-leg at dedicated stations, then runs a secondary reshaping pass so the finished shape does not depend on spring-back either. One operator loads bulk capacitors into the vibratory bowl; the parts come out at about one thousand an hour.

Keep the capability split as a recurring check rather than a one-off study. Repeat it when a new operator joins, when a die is resharpened, and when the capacitor supplier changes. Three repetitions a year is enough to know whether your process is drifting, and cheap enough that nobody argues about the time.

If you have two populations and you want them merged, send twenty parts from each operator to info@smthelp.com. We will measure them, show you the separation, and tell you whether a die change or a fixture change is the honest answer.

ARTICLE 04Why your insertion machine keeps rejecting hand-formed parts

The inserter is usually blamed for a rejection rate that was set upstream. Three checks tell you whether the forming bench is the real bottleneck.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine figures quoted inside them come from the S-EPCOS technical agreement; part dimensions come from the customer’s capacitor drawing.

The insertion machine stops, the operator clears a part, and the log says misaligned lead. Nobody writes down that the part was formed by hand two rooms away, forty minutes earlier, by someone who was working to a lever rather than to a dimension. The inserter gets the reputation. The forming bench keeps its schedule.

Here is what the reject actually costs. Every rejected part is a capacitor that was already formed, already counted, and already paid for. Clearing it stops the inserter, which stops the line. Then somebody has to sort the parts that were formed in the same batch, because you cannot tell by looking which ones are outside tolerance. That sort is the expensive part, and it does not appear in the reject rate at all.

The method is to run three checks before blaming the machine. First, take the last twenty rejected parts and measure the same two dimensions on all of them. If they share a direction of error, the forming is biased. Second, take twenty accepted parts from the same batch and measure them the same way. If the accepted parts are also drifting toward the limit, you are running at the edge of tolerance and the rejection is inevitable. Third, measure the pad pitch on the board and compare it with the formed lead span. A board change nobody told the forming bench about will look exactly like a machine fault.

The tool that removes the bias is a formed part produced by a die rather than by a lever. When the die is cut to the capacitor drawing and the forming happens at dedicated stations on an indexer, the lead span is a property of the die, not of the shift. The S-EPCOS machine was built for exactly this case: bulk capacitors in on a vibratory rail, lead cut, X and Y ninety-degree bends, K-leg, secondary reshaping, and formed parts out on a conveyor at about one thousand pieces an hour, with the die cut to the customer's drawing so part ten matches part one thousand.

Come back to the three checks whenever the reject rate moves, not only when it becomes a crisis. A bias that is caught at twenty rejected parts is a die adjustment. The same bias caught at two thousand rejected parts is a delivery date.

Send us the rejected parts and the board. We will measure both, tell you which side of the interface moved, and put the numbers in a one-page report you can take to your own customer.

ARTICLE 05Loose bulk capacitors are cheaper until you form them by hand

Bulk parts win on the purchase order and lose on the bench. The honest comparison is cost per finished, inserted part, not cost per capacitor.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine figures quoted inside them come from the S-EPCOS technical agreement; part dimensions come from the customer’s capacitor drawing.

Bulk capacitors are cheaper per piece than taped ones. Everybody knows that, and the purchasing decision usually stops there. What the purchase order does not show is the bench that has to turn loose parts into formed parts, and the labour that bench consumes every shift.

The gap widens with the part size. A large electrolytic takes longer to pick up, longer to seat in a jig, and longer to check than a small ceramic, and the forming step is where the extra time goes. If you are forming a few hundred large capacitors a shift by hand, you have quietly bought a second process, and it is staffed by people who could be doing something the machine cannot do.

The comparison that tells the truth is cost per finished part, and it has three terms. Material cost per piece. Forming labour per piece, which is the loaded wage divided by the parts one operator finishes in an hour. And rejection cost per piece, which is the material cost multiplied by the reject rate and divided by the yield. Write the three down for bulk and for taped, and the answer is usually not the one the purchase order suggested.

Bulk still wins, but it wins on the forming side, not the material side. A machine that takes loose capacitors straight from a vibratory bowl and returns cut, bent and K-legged parts removes the manual forming step entirely, which is the term that was carrying the cost. The S-EPCOS machine does exactly that in one eight-station pass at roughly one thousand parts an hour, with one operator loading the bowl, and the die cut to the customer's own capacitor drawing.

Re-run the three-term comparison when your monthly volume changes by more than a third. Below a few thousand pieces a month the manual bench is genuinely cheaper and we will say so. Above it, the labour term starts to dominate and the arithmetic flips.

Send us your capacitor part number, your monthly quantity and your loaded wage to info@smthelp.com. We will run the three terms on your numbers and tell you whether a machine or a bench is the right answer for your volume.

ARTICLE 06What one thousand pieces an hour actually buys you

A capacity figure on its own is marketing. Turn it into parts per shift, shifts per order and orders per month, and it becomes a planning number you can defend.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine figures quoted inside them come from the S-EPCOS technical agreement; part dimensions come from the customer’s capacitor drawing.

One thousand pieces an hour is the kind of number that gets printed on a brochure and never used again. It is also, once you do three multiplications, the number that decides whether you can take a large order without hiring anybody.

The trap is treating it as a monthly capacity. A machine that runs at one thousand an hour only produces one thousand an hour while it is running, and it is not running while the bowl is being refilled, while a die is being changed, or while the line is waiting for boards. Factories that plan against the brochure figure take orders they cannot ship, and then blame the machine.

The method is to convert the rate into three figures you can defend. Parts per shift is the rate multiplied by the hours the machine is actually attended. Parts per day is that figure multiplied by the number of shifts. Parts per month is that figure multiplied by working days, then reduced by a derating factor you choose deliberately. Pick a derating you are willing to write down, and use the same one every time so the comparisons stay honest.

The S-EPCOS machine is quoted at about one thousand parts an hour in the technical agreement, which is where the figure on this page comes from. What the machine changes is not just the rate but the shape of the labour: one operator loads the vibratory bowl and the indexer does the cutting, the X and Y ninety-degree forming, the K-leg forming and the secondary reshaping. That is why the shift figure scales with attended hours rather than with headcount.

Revisit the derating factor every quarter and keep the history. A derating that creeps upward is a signal about refill frequency, die changes or board supply, and all three are cheaper to fix than a missed order.

Send us your monthly volume and your shift pattern to info@smthelp.com. We will turn the rate into a shift plan, show you where the derating bites, and tell you honestly whether one machine covers your peak.

ARTICLE 07When the pad moves, the die has to move with it

Board revisions are the quiet killer of forming processes. The capacitor did not change, so nobody tells the forming bench, and the parts stop fitting.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine figures quoted inside them come from the S-EPCOS technical agreement; part dimensions come from the customer’s capacitor drawing.

The board revision lands on a Thursday. A pad moves two millimetres to make room for a taller component, the change is approved, the new boards arrive, and the insertion machine starts rejecting parts. The capacitor is the same capacitor. The forming bench is the same bench. Nothing in the forming process looks wrong, because nothing in the forming process changed.

This is the most expensive class of forming fault because it is invisible until the parts meet the board. The lead span, the leg angle and the K-leg depth are all still inside the drawing. They are simply inside the drawing for a pad position that no longer exists. Every party in the chain is measuring against a document that is one revision old, and the mismatch only surfaces at the last station.

The method is to couple the two documents. Whenever a PCB revision is released, the forming drawing gets a review, and the review has one question: did any dimension that the leads touch change? Pad pitch, pad diameter, board thickness, component height and the position of the neighbouring part all qualify. If the answer is yes, the die gets checked before the next batch is formed, not after the first rejection.

That review is only cheap if the forming process is a die. A die can be modified or replaced as a discrete item, and the change is verifiable because the die geometry is the reference. A hand jig can be adjusted too, but the adjustment is not repeatable, so a revision change turns into a slow drift rather than a step. The S-EPCOS machine is built around this assumption: the die set is cut to the customer’s capacitor drawing, so a drawing change is a die change and nothing else.

Put the revision review on the engineering change process itself, so it fires automatically. A forming review that depends on somebody remembering is a review that happens after the first rejected batch.

Send the old board and the new board together with the forming drawing to info@smthelp.com. We will measure the difference, tell you which die dimension needs to change, and quote the change separately from any machine cost.

ARTICLE 08The five-minute check that catches forming drift

Five minutes at the start of a shift, five measurements on one part, written on a card. That is the whole system, and it beats a quarterly audit.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine figures quoted inside them come from the S-EPCOS technical agreement; part dimensions come from the customer’s capacitor drawing.

Five minutes at the start of a shift. One formed part off the conveyor, measured on five dimensions, written on a card that lives on the machine. That is the entire routine, and it prevents more scrap than any audit you can schedule.

Most forming problems are caught late because the only measurement in the system is the one taken after a rejection. By then the parts have already been formed, counted and paid for. What is missing is a reading that is taken while the process is healthy, so that a change has something to be a change from.

The method has five steps and they take five minutes. Take one part from the start of the shift. Measure the cut length, the bend-to-bend distance, the leg angle, the K-leg depth and the overall envelope. Write all five on the card with the time. Compare with yesterday's card. If any figure has moved by more than a third of its tolerance, stop and look before running the batch.

The check only works if the measurements are easy to take, which is the reason a die-based process is easier to monitor than a manual one. On a machine that forms at fixed stations the five dimensions are stable from part to part, so a single part is a representative sample. On a hand jig the same five minutes produces a number that describes one part and nothing else, and the operator knows it.

Keep the cards. Six months of cards turns into a drift chart without anybody collecting data on purpose, and a die that is starting to wear shows up as a slow line rather than as a crisis. The cards also become the evidence when a customer asks how you control the process.

Send us your five dimensions and we will tell you which one is most likely to move first on your part, and what tolerance band to write on the card. Reply comes from info@smthelp.com.

14 — FAQ

The questions this machine raises

What exactly does the machine do to the capacitor?
It cuts both leads, forms an X-direction 90° bend, forms a Y-direction 90° bend, forms the K-leg and runs a secondary reshaping pass, then discharges the finished part onto a conveyor. The sequence is quoted step for step from the technical agreement.
How fast is it, and how many operators does it need?
The agreement quotes about 1,000 pieces an hour. The loading structure is manual feed into a vibratory bowl with automatic alignment and a material sensor, so one operator keeps the bowl supplied while the indexer does the forming.
Can it run a capacitor that is not an EPCOS part?
The machine is built around a part, and this project is built around one customer's capacitor and forming drawing. A different capacitor needs its own die set and bowl tooling. Send the drawing and a sample and we will tell you exactly what changes.
The air supply figure looks wrong. Which is it?
The agreement says 5–7 MPa, which would be 50–70 bar and is far outside normal workshop practice for a machine of this class. We believe it is a decimal slip for 0.5–0.7 MPa. It is listed as to be confirmed, and we will not ship against a guess.
Is there a catalogue model number?
This is a non-standard machine built for a specific capacitor. The document metadata carries the designation BT-320, a machine from the same family, but the body text states no model. We call it S-EPCOS, the project name, and will only quote a catalogue model once it is confirmed.
What does it need on site?
AC 220 V ±10 % at 50 Hz, a compressed-air supply, and roughly 1,800 × 1,200 mm of floor with about 1,900 mm of height for a machine weighing about 190 kg. Allow clear access to the bowl for refilling and to the tooling for die changes.
How do I know the die will hold the tolerance?
Because a die holds a dimension by geometry rather than by attention. We measure a sample of formed parts across the five critical dimensions and give you the spread, so capability becomes a number you can check rather than a claim you have to accept.
How do I get a quotation?
Send the capacitor drawing, the forming requirement, your monthly quantity and a sample of the part to info@smthelp.com or on WhatsApp. The quotation comes back with the die scope and the machine configuration separated, so you can see what you are buying.
